Prostitute
PROS-ti-toot
v. (to give over to unlawful use; to expose for hire)
Hebrew chalal, to profane, to make common — the same verb used of profaning the sabbath and the sanctuary. Latin prostituere, to set forth in public, to expose for sale. The Hebrew is the more revealing: to prostitute is to make common what was holy.

Biblical Definition

Do not prostitute thy daughter, to cause her to be a whore; lest the land fall to whoredom, and the land become full of wickedness. The command is addressed to fathers, and the Hebrew verb is the key to it. Chalal means to profane — to take something set apart and make it common. Scripture's objection to this trade is therefore not squeamishness about the body but the desecration of a person made in God's image and entrusted to a father's protection. The cultic background is real: the surrounding nations attached prostitution to their temples, and Israel is forbidden it in those terms as well — there shall be no whore of the daughters of Israel, nor a sodomite of the sons of Israel. The reason given in the verse deserves attention because it runs against the modern instinct entirely. The prohibition is grounded not only in the harm to the daughter but in what it does to the nation: lest the land fall to whoredom, and the land become full of wickedness. Scripture assumes that private transactions have public consequences and that a land can be defiled by what its households permit. Sexual sin in the Bible is never merely a matter between consenting parties, and the law addresses the man with the power, which here is the father who could sell his own child.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): to offer to a lewd use, or to indiscriminate lewdness; to devote to any base purpose; to give up to a low use.

expand to see more

PROSTITUTE, v.t. To offer freely to a lewd use, or to indiscriminate lewdness.

PROSTITUTE, v.t. To devote to any thing base; to give up to any vile purpose; as, to prostitute talents to the propagation of vice.

PROSTITUTE, n. A female given to indiscriminate lewdness; a strumpet.

PROFANE, v.t. To violate any thing sacred, or treat it with abuse, irreverence or contempt; to put to a wrong or unworthy use.

WHOREDOM, n. The practice of unlawful commerce with the other sex; in Scripture, idolatry.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 19:29 — "Do not prostitute thy daughter, to cause her to be a whore; lest the land fall to whoredom, and the land become full of wickedness."

Deuteronomy 23:17 — "There shall be no whore of the daughters of Israel, nor a sodomite of the sons of Israel."

Hebrews 13:4 — "Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge."

Ezekiel 16:8 — "Now when I passed by thee, and looked upon thee, behold, thy time was the time of love; and I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine."

Modern Corruption

The trade is relabelled as work freely chosen between consenting adults, and its industrialised form is consumed privately at enormous scale; Scripture calls it profaning a person and holds that a land is defiled by it.

expand to see more

The contemporary case rests on consent and autonomy: what adults agree to is nobody else's concern, and the trade is best understood as labour deserving recognition rather than prohibition. Leviticus 19:29 denies both premises. The Hebrew verb says a person is being profaned, which is language of desecration rather than of contract, and the consequence named is public — lest the land fall to whoredom. Consent does not undo desecration; a man may agree to his own degradation and it remains degradation. The dictionary also notes what the verse assumes about the people involved: the daughter here is being disposed of by someone with power over her, which remains the ordinary shape of the trade in every century.

Pornography is this text's most obvious modern application and the one most often evaded, since no transaction appears to occur in the viewer's room. The trade is nonetheless there, industrialised, with real persons profaned at its source. And the corruption Leviticus warns of — a land grown full of wickedness — describes the downstream effects with uncomfortable accuracy: marriages hollowed, appetites trained toward what Scripture forbids, a generation catechised in a false account of the body. Against all of it Scripture sets not prudery but a high doctrine of the body and of marriage: marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chalal (H2490), to profane or make common; zanah (H2181), to play the harlot; qedeshah (H6948), a cult prostitute; zimmah (H2154), wickedness or lewd purpose.

expand to see more

Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to profane, to make common; rendered prostitute, and used of profaning the sanctuary.

Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit fornication, to play the harlot.

Hebrew qedeshah (H6948) — a consecrated woman, a temple prostitute; forbidden at Deuteronomy 23:17.

Hebrew zimmah (H2154) — a wicked purpose, lewdness; rendered wickedness.

Hebrew erets (H776) — the land; what falls to whoredom when households do.

Usage

"“do not prostitute thy daughter” — addressed to the man with the power."

"“lest the land fall to whoredom” — the public consequence of private trade."

"“marriage is honourable in all” — the doctrine set against it."
